Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

solve verb

find the answer to a problem or a puzzle

also work out (a problem), figure out, sort out (a difficulty), puzzle out

classical

Quint. 8.6.53: aenigmata (Lewis & Short)
Val. Max. 9.12 ext. 3: quia quaestiōnem solvere nōn posset (Lewis & Short)

solvō, solvere, solvī, solūtum

verb, third conjugation, transitive

solve, clear up (a question, a riddle)

Lewis & Short: “of difficulties, riddles, questions, ambiguities, etc., to solve, explain, remove”, from Quintilian, Seneca and Valerius Maximus on. Cicero uses dissolvere of refuting an argument. The everyday senses of solvere are to untie, to set free and, above all, to pay (see pay).

Other words

  • explicō, explicāre, explicāvī, explicātum — sort out, settle (something tangled or difficult)

    verb, first conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 13.26.2: ut ejus negōtia explicēs et expediās (Lewis & Short)

    Literally to unfold or unroll; of affairs, to disentangle and settle them (Lewis & Short). It also means to explain (see explain).

  • expediō, expedīre, expedīvī, expedītum — get out of a difficulty; work out, explain

    verb, fourth conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Cic. Pis. 74: haerērem, nisi tū mē expedīssēs (Lewis & Short); Phaedr. 3.14.6: expedī quid fēcerim

    Literally to free the feet from a snare; so to free someone from a difficulty, or to get a matter straight. With a question, to work out and tell the answer, as in Phaedrus.

Examples

  • quia quaestiōnem solvere nōn posset

    because he could not solve the questionVal. Max. 9.12 ext. 3 (Lewis & Short)

  • petō ā tē, ut ejus negōtia explicēs et expediās

    I ask you to sort out and settle his affairsCic. Fam. 13.26.2 (Lewis & Short)

  • heus! inquit, sapiēns, expedī quid fēcerim

    “Come on, wise man,” he said, “work out what I have done”Phaedr. 3.14.6

See also problem, solution, riddle, explain.
